title: Offshore Petroleum (Safety Levies) Amendment (Greenhouse Gas Storage) Bill 2008

divisions.question: Consideration resumed from 16 October. [OFFSHORE PETROLEUM AMENDMENT (GREENHOUSE GAS STORAGE) BILL 2008](http://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/search/display/display.w3p;query=Id:legislation/billhome/R3030) Bill—by leave—taken as a whole. Penny Wong I table a supplementary explanatory memorandum relating to the government amendments to be moved to this bill. I am advised that the memorandum was circulated in the chamber on 14 October 2008. Christine Milne I move Australian Greens amendment (1) on sheet 5603 revised: (1) Schedule 1, item 2A, page 3 (after line 23), at the end of section 2A, add: (2) Another object of this Act is to ensure the full liability into the future for any adverse impact, including any leakage from carbon storage projects, is borne by the entities undertaking those projects. It is an additional subsection and the effect of this amendment is to include: Another object of this Act is to ensure the full liability into the future for any adverse impact, including any leakage from carbon storage projects, is borne by the entities undertaking those projects. The reason for this amendment is to make very clear in the objects of this legislation that the liability for leakage is borne by the entities that undertake the projects and cannot therefore be seen as being borne by the community. This is the most vexed issue of the whole thing around carbon capture and storage. Companies can go out and pump liquefied carbon dioxide into these cavities and get their closure certificate from the minister. But, as the current legislation stands, there is the question of liability. What if the liquefied carbon dioxide starts leaking out of these cavities 20 or 50 years later? You will then have massive volumes of carbon dioxide going into the atmosphere. speeches.speaker: Joe Ludwig
speeches.brief: Three bills were moved to amend offshore petroleum legislation, extending annual fees, registration fees, and safety levies to greenhouse gas titles, facilities, and pipelines.

The bills amend offshore petroleum legislation to establish a regulatory framework for greenhouse gas storage, including annual fees, registration fees, and safety levies. The debate resumed following Senator Ludwig's motion for a second reading.

speeches.speaker: Glenn Sterle
speeches.brief: The speaker argued that the Offshore Petroleum Amendment (Greenhouse Gas Storage) Bill 2008 establishes a regulatory framework for injecting and storing carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases in offshore geological formations, with particular opportunities off Western Australia's North West Shelf and Browse Basin. The speaker noted the Rudd government committed $200 million to a global carbon capture institute and cited support from Woodside, the Minerals Council of Australia, and British Prime Minister Gordon Brown.

speeches.speaker: Glenn Sterle
speeches.brief: The speaker supported the Offshore Petroleum Amendment (Greenhouse Gas Storage) Bill 2008, arguing it provides a necessary framework for carbon capture and storage (CCS) and noting Woodside’s role in Western Australia. Senator Bob Brown opposed the bill, stating CCS technology is unproven and that liability should rest with private companies, not the public, while urging immediate action on renewable energy and ending native forest logging.

speeches.speaker: Don Farrell
speeches.brief: The speaker argued for the Offshore Petroleum Amendment (Greenhouse Gas Storage) Bill 2008, which establishes a regulatory framework for offshore carbon capture and storage (CCS), and highlighted the government's $10.4 billion Economic Security Strategy, $500 million National Low Emissions Coal Fund, and a $1 billion industry COAL21 fund.

speeches.speaker: Penny Wong
speeches.brief: Senator Milne argued that the full liability for any adverse impact, including leakage from carbon storage projects, must be borne by the entities undertaking those projects, and moved amendments to entrench the polluter pays principle, require bonds for future liabilities, and establish expert advisory committees on environmental impacts. She cited the International Energy Agency report and examples of mining legacy issues such as the Fly River in Papua New Guinea and the King River in Tasmania.
